summary: For learners aged 7–9, build understanding of a rainforest food web: energy flows from producers (plants) to primary consumers (herbivores) to secondary consumers (predators), while decomposers (fungi, insects) break down dead material and recycle nutrients back to the soil. Core teaching goals are correct arrow direction (arrows mean 'energy flows TO the eater'), defining the three roles by test rather than label, moving from a single chain to an interconnected web, and reasoning about knock-on effects when a species is removed. A build-and-perturb activity is the lead approach, with a labelled reference web and sequence/matching tasks as complementary supports. Energy flows one way from the Sun and is lost as heat; only nutrients cycle.
misconceptions: 'Arrows point to who eats / to the prey' — arrows show energy flow, pointing toward the consumer.
'Decomposers are just rubbish/dead things' — they are active organisms that recycle nutrients.
'Big predators are producers because they're at the top' — confusing trophic position; only plants are producers.
'Removing one animal doesn't matter' — webs are interdependent; one loss can cascade.
'Energy is recycled like nutrients' — nutrients cycle, but energy flows one way from the Sun and is lost as heat.

activities.title: Build the web, then pull a thread
steps: Assemble a rainforest food web by placing the energy source and organisms: sunlight (the Sun), kapok leaves, a leaf-cutter ant, an anteater, a jaguar, and fungi on the forest floor.
Draw energy-flow arrows between them in the correct direction, starting Sun → kapok leaves → leaf-cutter ant → anteater → jaguar.
When you draw an arrow the wrong way (e.g. from the anteater TO the ant), respond to the prompt 'which way does the FOOD (energy) go?' and flip it to point toward the eater.
Connect the dead jaguar and fallen leaf litter to the fungi, and the fungi back to the soil and roots, closing the nutrient loop.

Remove the leaf-cutter ants from the web and observe what happens in this simplified model to the anteater (which eats the ants) and then the jaguar (which eats the anteater), so the cascade along the chain is visible. In a real rainforest, these animals also eat other food, so the effect would usually be smaller.
Explain in your own words why pulling out one species affects the others.
activities.insight: Producers, consumers and decomposers are not just a list of labels — they are connected to each other. Energy flows one way from the Sun toward each eater and is not recycled, while nutrients cycle back through decomposers to the soil for plants to reuse. Removing one species can affect others that depend on it, and the effect can pass along a chain.

activities.title: Label the web: roles and who eats whom
steps: Explore a labelled rainforest web diagram where tapping an organism reveals its role (producer, consumer or decomposer) and what eats it.
Use each role's TEST to justify the label: producer MAKES its own food by photosynthesis, consumer EATS others, decomposer BREAKS DOWN the dead.
Trace at least one full chain through the web and read the layout of the many interlinked chains.
activities.insight: The vocabulary (producer, consumer, decomposer) and web layout become a clear reference, defined by what each organism DOES rather than just a name or its position in the diagram.

activities.title: Order the chain and sort the roles
steps: Order a scrambled set of organisms into a correct chain (producer → herbivore → predator), placing an arrow at each link pointing toward the eater.
Sort a mixed set of rainforest organisms into producers, consumers and decomposers.
State for each sorted organism the test that justifies its group (makes food / eats others / breaks down the dead).
activities.insight: Being able to order a chain with correct arrows and categorise organisms by role confirms the vocabulary and sequencing are secure.

checkQuestion: In a food chain we draw an arrow between a leaf and a caterpillar that eats it. Which way should the arrow point — from the leaf to the caterpillar, or from the caterpillar to the leaf? Draw it, and then tell me WHY it points that way.
checkAnswer: The arrow points FROM the leaf TO the caterpillar. The arrow shows which way the energy (food) flows — from the thing being eaten to the eater — so it always points towards the animal doing the eating: leaf → caterpillar → bird, and so on. Decomposers like fungi and insects then break down dead things and return the nutrients to the soil for plants to use again.
